deed: Protalix grows a drug for Gaucher patients in carrot cells — the first made in genetically engineered plant cells to be approved by the FDA
title: Israel's Protalix grew an enzyme for Gaucher patients in carrot cells, and the FDA approved it

trailer.text: Protalix is an Israeli biotechnology company based in Carmiel.
People with Gaucher lack an important enzyme, and since 2009 they have been affected by disruptions in the supply of treatments in many countries.
Protalix scientists inserted the gene for the missing human enzyme into carrot cells, and in this way created it in the carrot cells.
The FDA approved the drug, Elelyso, and this is the first time it has approved a drug produced in a genetically engineered plant cell.

The disease disproportionately affects Ashkenazi Jews, and Protalix partnered with Pfizer for the exclusive commercialization of the drug worldwide except in Israel, where Protalix retained the exclusive rights.

stations.title: A rare disease and a missing enzyme

paragraphs.text: People with Gaucher lack an important enzyme.
Without it, fatty substances build up in the liver, spleen and nervous system, and this buildup is dangerous.
The disease shows itself in bruising, fatigue, anemia, low blood platelets and enlargement of the liver and spleen.
It can cause organ damage or death.
Gaucher affects about one in 50,000 to 100,000 people.
According to the FDA, type 1 Gaucher affects about 6,000 people in the United States.
In the United States, about one in a hundred people carry the common type of the disease, and among Ashkenazi Jews the carrier rate is 8.9 percent.
Israel therefore represents a relatively large share of the market.
Two other enzyme replacement therapies for Gaucher, imiglucerase and velaglucerase, were already on the market.
Disruptions in the supply of approved treatments have affected people with Gaucher since 2009 in many countries, including the United States.
According to GlobalData, the source of the Cerezyme shortage was a viral contamination incident at a Genzyme facility in Massachusetts.

Rhonda Buyers of the National Gaucher Foundation said that during the shortage, patients whose symptoms had been controlled for years suffered from bone problems and severe fatigue, and some ended up in the hospital.
David Aviezer, CEO of Protalix, said that the company's passion to develop the drug came from personal experience with family members and friends who live with the disease.

stations.title: A human enzyme inside a carrot cell

paragraphs.text: Protalix scientists developed a method to create in carrot cells the human enzyme that the patients lack.
They inserted into the cells the gene that encodes the protein.
The method relies on Protalix's manufacturing system, ProCellEx, in genetically engineered carrot cells.
The engineered carrot cells are grown in disposable 800-liter plastic bags.
Structurally, Elelyso resembles Genzyme's Cerezyme, but it is cheaper to produce, because animal-cell cultures require a great deal of maintenance.
Viruses and other pathogens that contaminate mammalian cell stocks do not threaten plant-cell cultures.
A pivotal Phase III clinical trial, on which the application for approval was based, was completed in September 2009.
In the clinical trials, patients treated with the enzyme fared at least as well as patients given the existing treatment, Cerezyme.
In a switchover study that lasted nine months, patients who switched from Cerezyme to Elelyso remained stable.
According to GlobalData, there were no concerns regarding the drug's efficacy or safety.
Pfizer and Protalix announced that the FDA had approved Elelyso (taliglucerase alfa) for the long-term treatment of adults with a confirmed diagnosis of type 1 Gaucher disease.
This is the first time the FDA has approved a drug produced in a genetically engineered plant cell.
Protalix presents Elelyso as the first FDA-approved drug made from a genetically engineered plant.
The FDA and the EMA granted Elelyso orphan drug status.
According to the FDA, this means it treats a condition that affects fewer than 200,000 people in the United States.
With the approval, the companies received seven years of marketing exclusivity.

stations.title: Pfizer brings the drug to patients

paragraphs.text: Protalix licensed the drug to the pharma giant Pfizer.
Pfizer received exclusivity worldwide except in Israel, and in Israel Protalix retained the exclusive rights.
According to a report in Bloomberg, Pfizer paid Protalix $60 million for the agreement.
According to the same report, Pfizer agreed to pay a further $55 million when certain regulatory requirements were met.

The agreement was signed in 2009, and under it sixty percent of the profits from US sales went to Pfizer; in 2015 the agreement was amended, and since then Pfizer receives all revenue and bears all expenses outside Brazil.
At launch, Elelyso was priced at $150,000 per year of therapy, 25 percent less than Cerezyme's $200,000.
Pfizer said it would keep 24 months of inventory for the 1,500 to 2,000 patients treated in the United States.
Pfizer will cover the entire co-pay for the drug for eligible patients who have commercial health insurance.
Diem Nguyen of Pfizer said that Elelyso is an important addition to the company's rare disease portfolio.
A week earlier, Shire, maker of the rival drug Vpriv, said it had not received FDA approval to manufacture its drug at a new facility in Massachusetts.
A new drug could ease worries about a shortage in the Gaucher market, which is worth $2 billion.
Analysts estimated that the low price and Pfizer's marketing would help the drug win a significant share of this market, which is expected to reach $4.5 billion by 2016.

stations.title: What was said about the approval

paragraphs.text: Rhonda Buyers of the National Gaucher Foundation said she was delighted that the community would have more treatment options, especially after the supply shortages of recent years.
According to Nature, she hopes that Elelyso will help prevent shortages like those of 2009 and 2011.
Julie Beitz of the FDA said that the approval shows the FDA's commitment to developing treatments for rare diseases.
Scientists and manufacturers developing enzymes, antibodies and vaccines in plants say that the approval may make the regulatory process simpler for them.
Earlier, in 2006, the US Department of Agriculture approved a chicken vaccine produced in plant cells.
Before the announcement, analyst Ritu Baral said that the approval would be a huge proof of concept for the entire platform.
After the approval, Protalix shares jumped nearly 23 percent, to $7.60, in after-market trading.
At the time of the 2012 approval, David Aviezer was president and chief executive of Protalix in Carmiel.
He said that the company sees the news as a recognition of its technology for manufacturing in plant cells.
According to him, the approval proves that the technology can make a large number of proteins.
Aviezer was optimistic about other carrot-made drugs then in development at the company.
In early 2012, Protalix began to plan Phase I clinical trials for a protein to treat Fabry disease.
The FDA rejected the drug a year before the approval and asked the companies for more data.
Only after that did it approve it.
GlobalData does not anticipate that Elelyso will displace Cerezyme as the market leader.
According to GlobalData, it is also unlikely that Elelyso will bring Protalix significant revenue.

disagreements.question: On what day was the FDA approval published?

versions.says: According to Fox News, US regulators approved the drug on Tuesday
According to the joint Pfizer–Protalix release filed with the SEC, the approval was announced on May 1, 2012, a Tuesday

disagreements.question: In which years was there a shortage of Cerezyme?

versions.says: According to Nature, there were shortages in 2009 and in 2011, when patients relied on Cerezyme alone
According to GlobalData, the global shortage of Cerezyme was between 2009 and 2010

disagreements.question: In what cells are the existing Gaucher drugs produced?

versions.says: According to Nature, Genzyme and Shire produce the enzymes in mammalian cells
According to GlobalData, Cerezyme is produced in Chinese hamster ovary cells, and Vpriv in a human fibroblast cell line
